entries.title: Re-vendor shiplog: the hold retracts, and bookkeeping stays filtered [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
Two fixes in one copy, and this repository had neither.

The hold is applied at projection as well as at derivation, so it can retract
an entry already sealed public — the case claimyour.gold found, where an entry
quoting a bootstrap credential was served among 746 public entries. Visibility
is inside the digest, so re-deriving to change it is the restatement
append-only forbids; the entry now keeps its seal and stops being handed out.

And the bookkeeping filter tolerates the suffixes those subjects have grown.
It anchored on $ exactly, so adding [skip ci] to every emitted commit would
have started sealing each refresh as a shipped entry under agent/unattributed.

Holding is not remediation. A credential that reached a public history stays
burned until it is rotated.

Kind: fix

entries.title: backlog/1: refresh the fragment [skip ci]
Re-vendor shiplog: the hold can now retract an already-published entry [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
Visibility is inside an entry's digest, so an entry sealed public stays sealed
public — re-deriving it to change that is the restatement append-only forbids.
So a hold added afterwards changed nothing here: the entry kept being handed
out at the well-known URL.

claimyour.gold found the case. An entry explaining the removal of a bootstrap
credential quoted the token and the admin password verbatim, and was being
served among 746 public entries.

The fix applies the hold at projection as well as at derivation, so the record
keeps its seal and the served copy honours the hold: the entry stays in the
fragment, digest intact, counted, and simply stops being handed out.

It existed in flashyos's own root copy and in no other repository. Twenty-eight
vendored the version without it — including the one where the incident
happened. This is that copy, replaced.

Holding is still not remediation. A credential that reached a public history
stays burned until it is rotated.

Kind: fix

shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it [skip ci]
Derived-log workflows survive a moving main; the served fragment matches the record
entries.detail:
The backlog and shiplog workflows carried a bare 'git push', which loses
the race whenever main moves under the run — the failure flashyos hit
three runs straight before growing the regenerate-on-the-new-tip retry
this ports. Rebase is deliberately not the retry: these artifacts derive
from the very history that moved.

Where this repository's served public/directory.fragment.json trailed
the committed record (the diff the Directory workflow refuses), the two
are re-synced from the emitter's output, with every directory check run
locally before committing.

entries.title: backlog/1: refresh the fragment [skip ci]
Serve the charter where the checker actually reads it [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
@flashyos/conformance reads a charter from /.well-known/flashyos-charter.json
and nowhere else. Holding one in the repository is a different fact from
serving one, and the estate has now got that wrong three times: nine properties
were fixed in August 2026 and the failure written up as closed; a read of every
default branch on 30 August found seven still holding a complete roster and
serving it nowhere; this property was one of them on 31 August.

Nothing failed. A conformance run against this domain simply stopped at L1
while the roster sat in git looking finished.

The served copy is byte-identical to the one this repository holds, and a test
pins that. Byte-identity rather than field-by-field, deliberately: a test that
checks the fields somebody thought to list says nothing about the field added
next week.

Kind: fix

entries.title: An emitted record must not spend a deploy [vercel skip]
entries.detail:
The emitters commit a refreshed fragment on every push, and each of those is a
deployment. On 2026-08-31 the estate landed 594 commits on default branches and
321 of them — 54% — were emitters refreshing their own output. Vercel's build
rate limit is 100 a day across the account, so the record-keeping machinery was
consuming the whole estate's deploy budget three times over and starving the
pushes people actually made.

It was invisible everywhere. Each property sat a few revisions behind, gda.group
had stopped on 30 August, nothing was red. The one place it was written down was
a commit status on a dependabot PR nobody had opened: "Deployment rate limited —
retry in 24 hours."

[skip ci] is the marker Vercel and GitHub Actions both honour. The fragment
still reaches the domain on the next deploy a real push triggers, which is the
right cadence for a record of something that already happened.

This commit carries [vercel skip] rather than [skip ci] so CI still validates
it without spending one of the deploys it exists to save.

Kind: fix

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
Stop declaring surfaces at a hostname that does not exist
entries.detail:
`SURFACE_HOST` fell back to the charter slug when a repository has no
property, which manufactures a hostname out of a repository name. This
repository is a library with no website, so its published record declared four
surfaces at `https://flashy-ledger/.well-known/...` — a URL that resolves for
nobody, in a document whose whole purpose is to tell a stranger where to look.

Nothing caught it because every check reads git: the files really are in
`public/`, the fragment really validates, and only a fetch finds out. It took
a tool that fetches, and this was the first thing it reported.

The Source is emitted without a URL now. Serving these files is true; saying
where somebody can GET them is not, and a declared surface that cannot be
fetched is a promise in the record with nothing behind it — the rule three
comments above it in the same file.

Kind: fix

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
Re-vendor the directory checker, which had drifted in twelve repositories
entries.detail:
`scripts/check-directory.mjs` is a copy of
`packages/directory/vendor-check-directory.mjs` in flashyos, under a different
name — and `estate-hygiene` matched vendored copies by the `vendor-*` filename
pattern, so it never compared this one. Twelve repositories were running a
copy old enough not to read `directory.externals.json` at all, which is the
file that tells a borrowed id from a dangling one.

Nothing failed. That is how a vendored file fails: not by breaking, but by
disagreeing about exactly the field somebody has just started writing.

Kind: chore

Re-vendor the backlog emitter: it can revise an item now
entries.detail:
`file` has taken `--wants` since the beginning and nothing could add them
afterwards, so every item filed across the estate — all of them filed without
wants — was permanently invisible to the matcher, which refuses an item that
names no `capabilitiesWanted`. A format whose central field is
write-once-at-creation is a format whose central field is empty.

`revise` changes everything about an item except its visibility. Promotion
stays a separate verb because it is a separate decision: it refuses anything
but a `person/` id, and folding it in would give a revision the power to
publish. Unmentioned fields are left alone — `close` is a revision too, and
clearing on absence would strip every want in the repository.

Copied byte-identical from flashyos rather than edited here. A stale vendored
file does not break; it disagrees, silently, about exactly the field somebody
has just added.

Kind: chore

entries.title: Declare the machine that files this repository's intentions
entries.detail:
Two machines write this repository's record and only one was declared.
`.shiplog/config.json` stamps `agent/<slug>-ci` on every sealed entry;
`.backlog/config.json` stamps `agent/<slug>-bot` on every filed item. Both
appear in published fragments. The second appeared in no declaration anywhere
in the estate.

It survived the `-ci` rollout because the declaration looked complete:
`recordEmitter` listed `backlog/1` among the record emitter's formats, so
everything comparing formats saw it named and stopped, and nothing compared the
signature. A declaration naming the right format and the wrong machine is
complete in every respect except the one that matters.

The record emitter's scope narrows to `shipped/1`, which is what it signs. The
backlog emitter is declared beside it with its own `operates` and its own
`delegatedTo` from the accountable human, bounded to `backlog/1`.

Two machines is not an artefact of tooling. The tenses are shaped differently
on purpose — an item decays and is never sealed, an entry is sealed and never
decays — and different things write them at different times: the seal on a push
to the default branch, the filing whenever somebody records an intention.

Both ids are read from the config that stamps them, never composed.

Kind: chore

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BEaXzktRU5ZPe3R2NY7CKD

entries.title: Declare the machine surfaces this property serves
entries.detail:
Every property in the estate serves the same handful of documents — a
handshake, a charter, backlog/1, shipped/1, checkpoint/1 — and said nothing
about them in its own record. That silence is most of why the estate measured
as thirty graphs rather than one: a fragment describing only its own
organisation has no reason to name anything another repository defines, so
nothing crossed a boundary except one person's name on a commit.

Serving a format is a fact about this repository; the format belongs to
flashyos. `cites` is the edge for referencing something somebody else
authored, so each of these is a real join rather than a manufactured one.

Detected from disk, never listed. A hand-kept list keeps claiming a surface
the day somebody deletes the file, and a declared surface that cannot be
fetched is worse than an undeclared one — a promise in the record with
nothing behind it.

`directory.externals.json` is emitted beside the fragment and names what this
repository borrows: the standards flashyos authors, and the person
gord-holdings is the authority for. `check-directory.mjs` reads it instead of
taking `--external` flags, so the list cannot drift from the emitter.

The vendored checker was also one revision behind the canonical copy in
flashyos and would have rejected an `engaged` edge. Re-vendored.

Kind: feature

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01FDosmV9fXV6oZ9NXe7PZ76

entries.title: Say whose authority the record emitter signs under
entries.detail:
`operates` says this organisation runs the machine that seals its record. It
does not say who answers for what the machine signs, and that is the fact a
signature rests on: an agent acts *for* somebody, the somebody answers, and an
agent with no stated bound is one nobody can say has exceeded anything.

`delegatedTo` is that edge — person to agent, carrying the same scope the
emitter operates under. It is the shape of a Flashy ID root grant, whose issuer
is the accountable human and whose scope a chain may only ever narrow. The
record states the delegation; the signed assertion that enforces it lives in
Flashy ID, and no signature belongs here, because proof never moves into the
record.

The edge type has been in the vocabulary since the vocabulary was written and
no fragment in the estate had ever used one. Writing the first exposed two
faults in flashyos that are fixed there: the rule required `scopes` where the
edge carries `scope`, so no delegation could have satisfied it, and the
flat-to-embedded conversion discarded every relationship attribute but two, so
an edge that stated what it owed was reported as missing it.

Kind: chore

Read the emitter id, do not derive it
entries.detail:
The declaration added moments ago used `${charter.slug}-ci` and was wrong here:
this repository signs its record with an id the charter slug does not produce,
so it declared an agent that matched no signature anywhere. A declaration that
matches nothing is indistinguishable from one that works — every check that
looks at shape passes, and the provenance number does not move.

The id now comes from `.shiplog/config.json`, which is the file that actually
stamps it. Two of ten repositories were affected: ClaimYour.Gold signs
`agent/claimyour.gold-ci` against a charter slug of `claimyour-gold`, and
dais-global signs `agent/dais-global-ci` against a slug of `dais`.

`tools/emitter-declaration.test.mjs` in flashyos now compares the declared id
against the stamped one, which is the check that was missing.

entries.title: Declare the machine that signs this repository's record
entries.detail:
Every sealed entry and every fragment here carries
`assertedBy: agent/<slug>-ci`, and until now that was an id nothing in the
estate declared. Across thirty properties it was 2,478 edges citing an agent
that formally did not exist — provenance that reads as provenance and carries
none, which is worse than an empty field, because the empty field is honest
about not knowing who made the claim.

Declared as an Agent the organisation `operates`, not as a charter role. A
role is a governance label the org answers for and it is rendered into the
handshake's advertised capabilities, so a "ci" role would tell the network
this organisation does continuous integration for other people.

The canonical form is `declareEmitters` in `@flashyos/directory`. It is
inlined here because `scripts/directory.mjs` is dependency-free by design, and
`tools/emitter-declaration.test.mjs` in flashyos is the drift test that keeps
the two in step.

Kind: feature

entries.title: shipped/1: refresh the log, and the checkpoint over it
Publish a front door, and serve the charter it points at
entries.detail:
This repository publishes a handshake and a shiplog and had no door: nothing
saying which lanes it opens, what it asks at each, or what it owes in return.
An organisation reachable on the mesh with no stated way in is a doorbell
wired to nothing.

The lanes are chosen from what this property actually is rather than copied
from a sibling. It opens the lanes it can answer and does not advertise one it
cannot.

Two things vendored byte-identical from the estate: the emitter and the
checker. `notAuthority` is carried verbatim and the checker rejects any door
that paraphrases it — a door quietly read as an authorisation is how this
stops being a front door and becomes a vulnerability.

The workflow also required something this repository did not do: serve the
charter. It existed at the repository root only, where a static deploy never
serves it, so `/flashyos.roles.json` would have 404d while the standard this
estate publishes tells everyone else to put exactly that path there. The
served copy is now committed and the workflow holds the two identical.

Every step of the workflow was run locally first, so it arrives green rather
than as an alarm on arrival.

Re-vendor the charter checker: it had drifted from the spec
entries.detail:
The vendored checker rejected renamedFrom, which the charter defines and the
role-rename sync reads; rejected a digit in a role name, which the spec's own
regex allows; and enforced no length bound at all, so the 24-character role
name cap was the one rule this pre-install check could not see.

Eleven byte-identical copies across the estate agreed with each other
perfectly and disagreed with @flashyos/aao in all four places. The monorepo
now runs both checkers over the same documents and fails on any disagreement
about the verdict.

This charter still passes.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Name a copyright holder, and stop granting what was never ours
entries.detail:
Two errors from the licence sweep of 2026-08-30, found by putting the
estate's licences in one register and comparing.

A LICENCE THAT NAMED NOBODY

Eleven repositories carried a bare Apache-2.0 text with no copyright line
at all. That is not a missing file — it is a file that answers the
question wrongly. It reads as a grant, and no reader can tell who made it
or whether they were entitled to. Every LICENSE now opens with the holder
and one line saying what the repository is.

AN OPEN LICENCE ON SOMEBODY ELSE'S PROPERTY

kopman-build and buildos are a construction firm's marketing site and the
application behind that engagement. Both carried AGPL-3.0-only, which
offers a client's own site to anyone willing to publish their changes.
Nobody decided that; it was the default that got reached for. Both are now
all rights reserved, held by Kopman Build, with a line saying ownership is
governed by the agreement between the firm and the studio rather than by
the file.

The same care had already been taken for marco.law an hour earlier and
then not taken here, which is the argument for a register rather than for
being more careful next time.

Eight further repositories moved from an unattributed Apache-2.0 to all
rights reserved: the org profile, the Terraform that can delete
production, three brand properties and the three Life repositories.
flashy-sdk is among them and its package.json already said UNLICENSED —
the LICENSE file had been contradicting its own manifest.

`tools/estate-licences.mjs` in flashyos is now the one declaration, and it
reports a checkout and a default branch separately, because conflating
those is the mistake this estate's tooling keeps making.

Kind: fix

Fail loudly on a fragment that exists and cannot be parsed
entries.detail:
The emitter treated an unparseable fragment as an absent one and built a head
over whatever else it could read. A conflicted fragment produced a
valid-looking head over nothing.

Kind: fix

entries.detail: Kind: chore

entries.title: Adopt checkpoint/1 — a tree head over what this repository seals
entries.detail:
An RFC 6962 Merkle root over the sealed claims already published here, served
beside them. Anyone holding the fragments can recompute it and see whether the
record still describes what it said it did.

The head is deliberately unsigned. A signature over a root computed and checked
by the same party is ceremony without a property — what makes history provably
append-only is a witness who is not us, and that is not built. The root catches
drift and after-the-fact edits, and nothing here claims more.

It is refreshed by the shiplog workflow rather than its own, so the head and
the log it commits to always move in one commit. A separate workflow would
leave a window in which the published root and the published record disagree,
and a reader hitting that window sees a forged-looking estate.

Kind: feature

entries.title: Merge main, then publish
entries.detail:
Another session adopted these formats here independently. Its author
table and its branch-agnostic workflows are better than mine and are
taken as-is; the emitter is mine, because it carries three things theirs
does not and one of them is load-bearing under their design.

An emit is now a union rather than a replacement. Their workflow fires on
any push and gates the job on the default branch, which is the right fix
for the branch-pinning trap — but combined with derive-and-overwrite it
would let a feature branch rewrite the trunk’s log with its own
first-parent shape. Together the two changes are safe.

Also mine: .shiplog/held.json, so publishing a log is not the same
decision as publishing every entry in it; a guard that stops an agent’s
commits being filed under a person; and a filter for this format’s own
refresh commits, which were being recorded as things that shipped.

visibility is now public. That is the decision that turns an internal
record into a changelog anyone can read.

Kind: other

entries.title: Publish the log: 282 entries across the estate become public
entries.detail:
Everything derived has landed private since adoption. This flips
visibility for the estate-owned properties, which is the decision that
turns an internal record into a public changelog.

Two entries are held back by .shiplog/held.json, with the reason written
next to each: one names a credential that is still unrotated, one is a
frank internal note about a durability gap in a live product. Held, not
deleted — both are still in this repository’s own record, sealed and
counted. Only whether a stranger can read them changes.

The vendored emitter is re-copied in the same commit. The hold did
nothing until it was: the previously vendored copy predated the feature
and published the held entry regardless, silently.

Kind: feat

entries.title: Adopt the two tenses: what this repository intends, and what it shipped
entries.detail:
`backlog/1` and `shipped/1`, both emitted by a vendored, dependency-free
script and refreshed by a workflow on this repository's default branch.

Everything lands private. The served fragment publishes nothing until
somebody changes one field, which is the decision that turns an internal
log into a public changelog — not a side effect of adopting.

The log credits the agents that wrote the commits. That needed a fix
upstream first: with an empty `authors` table every unrecognised address
fell through to `defaultAuthor`, and the estate's first derived log read
100% human-authored over a history that was 95/107 agent-authored. `adopt`
now seeds the machine addresses it finds in the history.

The workflow triggers on the branch `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`
reports, which is not always `main` in this estate and is never the branch
adoption happened on.

Kind: feat

entries.title: Stop pinning the shiplog and backlog workflows to a branch name
entries.detail:
Each workflow triggered on `branches: ['<the default branch at adoption>']`.
Eleven repositories in this estate have a `claude/*` branch as their GitHub
default; renaming one to `main` is the right thing to do and would have stopped
its workflow firing. Nothing would have failed — the fragment would simply have
stopped advancing, and a stale changelog reads exactly like a current one.

The trigger now matches any push and the job is gated on
`github.ref_name == github.event.repository.default_branch`, resolved per run,
so a rename is survived rather than discovered. `branch` is dropped from the
config: nothing read it, and a stored branch name is a snapshot of something
that changes.

Kind: fix

entries.title: Reclassify the log against the convention this estate writes in
entries.detail:
The derived log was classified only by conventional-commit prefixes, and
this repository writes declarative English. Unclassified went from 96%
to 21% by reading the estate's declared imperative lexicon, looking
past a project prefix to the verb behind it, and dropping merges of
another branch into this line — which are not things that shipped.

Nothing is published: entries remain private and the served copy is the
public projection.

Ten of thirty-five repositories in the estate had a secret scan, and each
carried its own private copy. flashy-infra's CLAUDE.md said the estate consumed
a shared template; no repository referenced it, and the file was not a reusable

Verified against this repository's working tree before being added: a scan

This repository now publishes the two tenses the estate records: what it
intends, and what it shipped. Both are emitted by a dependency-free

entries land private until someone changes one field in

emitter writes it, so a private record cannot reach a URL through a

entries.title: Serve the directory fragment, which this property was not doing
entries.detail:
The fragment lived only at the repository root. A Next.js app does not
serve the repository root, so https://<this property>/directory.fragment.json
returned 404 — and the estate's directory is federated, meaning every
property is supposed to publish its own fragment for anyone to fetch and
merge.

Thirteen of fourteen properties were in this state. The consequence is
larger than a missing file: the estate graph could only be assembled by
someone with a git checkout of every repository, which defeats the entire
reason for federating it. A graph you can only build from a laptop proves
the files are on that laptop. A graph assembled from published URLs proves
the estate publishes what it says it does, can be reproduced by somebody
who does not trust us, and is the only shape that lets an organisation we
do not own ever join it.

Same defect as the charter, found the same way and fixed the same way: the
fragment is copied into the served directory and CI diffs the served copy
against the source so the two cannot drift.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01BEaXzktRU5ZPe3R2NY7CKD

entries.title: Make every charter in the estate conform, and gate it
entries.detail:
Ran the estate's own published validator - validateCharterDocument from
@flashyos/aao - against every charter for the first time. None passed,
including FlashyOS's own production charter and flashy-academy's. Two real
classes of failure:

  _comment is not part of aao 0.1. The spec's own extension convention is an
  x- prefix, and the validator says so in the error. Ten charters carried a
  bare key the standard does not recognise.

  Four family names were invented: trust, release, inbound, network-effects.
  The ten declared families are growth, revenue, product, engineering,
  operations, data, finance, risk, governance, support. Remapped trust to risk
  (compliance, security, audit), release to engineering, and inbound and
  network-effects to growth.

10/10 charters now clean against the published validator.

Adds scripts/check-charter.mjs, mirroring the static half of the conformance
suite, dependency-free so it runs before an install, vendored byte-identical
across the estate. Wired into the Directory workflow ahead of the fragment
check. The published validator stays authoritative; when @flashyos/agent is
available, `npx @flashyos/agent conform` supersedes this.

Verified against six failure modes, all caught: a bare non-spec key, an
invented family, a codename role, the template placeholder as accountable
human, a capability naming a department rather than an action, and an
escalation pointing at no declared role.

One correction along the way: the checker first flagged CRITICAL as an invalid
approval threshold in flashyos and flashy-ledger. IMPACT_ORDER is LOW, MEDIUM,
HIGH, CRITICAL - the charters were right and the checker was wrong. Fixed.

metaverse-group gains the charter it never had: six roles, four families left
deliberately empty, and its emitter now reads the charter so the two cannot
disagree.

11 fragments, 199 nodes, 188 edges, 100% freshness, zero errors.

entries.title: Gate the directory fragment in CI, in the repository that produces it
entries.detail:
The estate-wide merge catches contested authority and dangling references, but
it runs elsewhere and cannot say which repository caused them. This runs here,
on every push, and fails at the point the mistake is made.

scripts/check-directory.mjs is dependency-free on purpose - a validator that
needs an install is a validator that gets skipped. It is vendored byte-identical
into every repository in the estate; repository-specific values are passed as
--external flags rather than edited in, so the copies cannot drift.

.github/workflows/directory.yml runs three steps: emit from the charter, check
the fragment, then `git diff --exit-code` on the committed fragment. The third
is the one that matters - a committed fragment differing from a freshly emitted
one means someone edited the JSON instead of the source it comes from.

Verified against six real failure modes, each caught with the right code:
a claim defined twice, a deleted accountability edge, a reference to a node
nobody emits, an expiry before its assertion, an ownership edge with no
instrument, and hand-reordered nodes.

Eleven repositories still merge clean: 193 nodes, 182 edges, 100% freshness.

entries.title: Emit this repository's directory fragment
entries.detail:
Reads flashyos.roles.json and emits the organisation, each declared role as an
agent, the accountability edge, and the properties this repository operates.
The charter and the fragment cannot disagree because the fragment is generated
from the charter.

References person/michael rather than defining it - only repo/gord-holdings is
the authority for people. Merges clean with the rest of the estate.

entries.title: Publish with the PAT again; E409 never proved GITHUB_TOKEN could publish
entries.detail:
The registry checks version-existence before it verifies the token, so
run 12 reaching E409 proved nothing about auth. Every dispatch since
the GITHUB_TOKEN-first flip (0.6.3, 0.8.0) died with the same E401 on
the PUT while npm ci in the same runs read the package fine: the token
can read but not publish, because the package was created by manual PAT
publishes and its own access list decides who may PUT new versions.

entries.title: 0.8.0 — the Merkle spec becomes the package's, not one repo's
entries.detail:
Ported verbatim from flashy-network's src/lib/merkle.ts. The producer
(ClaimYour.Gold's nightly anchor) and the verifier (flashynetwork.com)
must hash identically or every published root stops verifying; two
copies of the same spec is how that failure arrives silently, and one
package is how it cannot.

Domain separation, byte-wise id sort and promoted-not-duplicated odd
nodes are unchanged. Index reads are guarded for this package's
noUncheckedIndexedAccess; the pinned-vector tests hard-code the
canonical string, a leaf digest and a three-entry root, so any change
to the bytes fails loudly as the format break it would be.

entries.title: 0.7.0 — declare the civilization commodities, and stop XP changing hands
entries.detail:
Two additions, both moving a rule out of prose and into the package.

WHEAT, WOOD, STONE and IRON join the registry. ClaimYour.Gold has
carried them as four Asset rows and a hand-written slug map since before
this registry existed, which is the exact shape the registry was built
to end: the same asset declared twice is the same asset until somebody
edits one of them. Zero decimals is not a display preference — amounts
are hashed as minor units, so a disagreement there reinterprets every
historical entry.

postTransfer refuses a non-transferable asset class. The asset-class
comment has said XP is never convertible since the experience domain
landed and nothing checked it; a sentence in a comment and a check in
postTransfer are not the same artefact, and only one survives a
contributor who has not read the comment.

Re-cut from 0.6.0 to 0.7.0: main released an asset registry as 0.6.0
while this was in flight and has since reached 0.6.3.

Two existing tests needed fixing rather than working around. One used
'wheat' as its example of an unknown slug — an absence test whose subject
quietly becomes real stops testing absence. The other built a defineAsset
fixture called wheat that now shadows a declared asset; it is barley.

entries.title: 0.6.0 — a skill asset cannot change hands
entries.detail:
The asset-class comment has said XP is 'never convertible' since the
experience domain landed, and experience.ts states the ledger enforces
the half it can see. Nothing did.

postTransfer now rejects any asset whose class is not transferable, and
produces no entries when it does. SKILL_XP is the only such class today;
currency, commodities and partner credit still move, because raids and a
marketplace need them to.

Consumption is left open on purpose. Whether XP can be spent is a product
decision somebody should have to write down; what this forecloses is XP
changing hands.

entries.title: 0.3.0 — experience settles on these books, and XP cannot be given away
entries.detail:
Folds the experience domain in from an unreleased fork that shipped as
@flashy/ledger@0.2.0: the same version number as this package's 0.2.0
with different contents, because it branched before tenant isolation.
Its consumer only used the pure domain functions, so 0.2.0's breaking
store changes do not touch it.

Five SKILL_XP assets at zero decimals, ids pinned by a literal test
because they go into every entry hash. xpIdempotencyKey() puts the key
convention in one function so ClaimYour.Gold and Flashy Academy derive
it identically and the second product to award a lesson collides rather
than pays again.

postTransfer now rejects non-transferable classes. The fork carried a
doc comment saying the ledger enforced the XP/currency separation while
no code did; skill assets moving between identities is a market in
status, which is a currency by another name.

entries.detail:
main renamed the package to @flashylabs/ledger in package.json only, so the
README and the entry-point docblock still told a reader to install a scope that
does not exist. Anyone copy-pasting the install line got nothing.

The changelog also claimed 0.1.0 was the first tagged release, which was true
when this branch was cut and stopped being true while it was open — v0.1.0,
v0.1.1 and v0.1.2 are all published. Backfilled from the commits on main so the
0.2.0 entry sits on an accurate history rather than an invented one.

entries.title: Drop the release workflow; main already publishes via publish.yml
Make tenancy a boundary instead of a label
entries.detail:
tenantId was written onto every asset and every entry — the comment above it
already read "which network's books this asset belongs to" — and used in no
query, no index and no type signature. With one tenant that is harmless. With
two it is three money bugs, and two of them are unique indexes on a collection
that would by then hold production entries.

The worst was idempotency. Keys derive from source events; this package's own
example is quest:q_9:identity_1, so two networks running similar mechanics
collide by construction. Globally scoped, a second tenant's legitimate award
found the first tenant's entry and returned it as a successful deduplication —
a lost award and a cross-tenant disclosure in the same code path, reporting
success. The chain-head constraint had the same shape: two tenants' first
entries for one identity both carry previousHash null, and the second was
refused as a duplicate. And reads folded across tenants, so a balance became
the sum of two networks' books.

Reads now take a scope object rather than positional strings. Three same-typed
parameters are transposable and this one decides whose money you are looking at,
so AccountRef and HistoryRef make the tenant impossible to omit and impossible
to put in the wrong slot. There is no overload without one.

ensureIndexes() drops the pre-0.2 indexes by name before creating the scoped
ones. This is the part that would otherwise have been missed: a surviving
uniq_idempotency still rejects a second tenant's legitimate write even though
the new index permits it, so creating the new indexes without removing the old
would look like a migration and behave like none.

Six isolation cases in the conformance suite, run against every adapter —
isolation is a property of the port, and a reference implementation that
isolates while the database adapter does not is worse than neither doing it.
Four of the six were verified to fail against the pre-fix implementation by
reverting the change and watching them go r

entries.title: rename scope to @flashylabs to match the GitHub account
entries.detail:
Every publish attempt so far has failed on the actual npm publish step,
even with a correctly-scoped PACKAGES_TOKEN (repo + write:packages).
GitHub Packages requires the npm scope to exactly match the GitHub
account that owns the repo — this repo is under FlashyLabs, not flashy,
so @flashy/ledger could never resolve to a real installation. Testing
the fix on this package alone before renaming @flashy/identity and
anything downstream.

entries.title: Bump @flashy/ledger to 0.1.1 to cut a clean release tag
entries.detail:
v0.1.0 was tagged before the PACKAGES_TOKEN publish fix existed, and
moving that tag over an unreliable connection kept failing silently.
A fresh version+tag avoids re-pushing over an existing ref.

entries.title: CUT-1: publish with a PAT instead of GITHUB_TOKEN
entries.detail:
GITHUB_TOKEN's Packages authorization was returning 403 'The requested
installation does not exist' on every publish attempt, identically on
this repo and on flashy-contracts, despite an otherwise correct
workflow. Switching NODE_AUTH_TOKEN to a classic PAT (PACKAGES_TOKEN
secret, write:packages scope) to get past it.

entries.title: CUT-1: automate publishing @flashy/ledger to GitHub Packages
entries.detail:
The package itself was already publish-ready — package.json already had
the right name, publishConfig (npm.pkg.github.com, restricted access),
and repository field. What was missing was any way to actually run
`npm publish` without someone doing it by hand from a machine with a
personal GH Packages token.

Tag-triggered (push a v0.1.0-shaped tag), not push-to-main-triggered —
a merge shouldn't be indistinguishable from a release. Uses the
workflow's own GITHUB_TOKEN with an explicit packages: write
permission rather than a manually-created NPM_TOKEN secret — nothing
to provision, rotate, or leak. Verifies the tag matches package.json's
version before publishing, so a forgotten version bump fails the job
instead of shipping under the wrong version number.

This is CUT-2's actual prerequisite: flashygoldams currently vendors
this package's build output into vendor/flashy-ledger specifically
because it isn't published anywhere reachable. Once a tag is pushed
and this runs once, that vendoring (and flashy-network's separate
github:-URL + Vercel GIT_CREDENTIALS workaround) can be retired.

entries.title: Ship a CommonJS build alongside the ESM one
entries.detail:
ClaimYour.Gold runs Jest with ts-jest, which transforms .ts and leaves .js
in node_modules alone. An ESM-only package therefore fails at parse time
with "Unexpected token 'export'" pointing at the importing test file, not
at the package — and relaxing transformIgnorePatterns does not help,
because ts-jest has no .js transform to apply.

Widening the peer range let the package install; this is what lets it be
used. Both were blocking the same consumer.

dist-cjs gets its own package.json declaring "type": "commonjs". The root
declares "type": "module", which applies to every .js beneath it, so Node
would otherwise load the CommonJS output as ESM and fail with "exports is
not defined" — a message that reads like a bug in the package rather than a
build configuration problem. The alternative was renaming every emitted
file to .cjs and rewriting its internal requires.

entries.title: Accept mongodb 7, and make the peer optional
entries.detail:
ClaimYour.Gold is on mongodb 7 and this package peered on ^6.21.0, so the
install failed outright — the first real consumer could not take the
dependency at all.

The range now spans both majors because the adapters use only driver APIs
that did not change between them: collection, createIndex, insertOne,
findOne, find/sort/limit/toArray, startSession, withTransaction,
endSession. Checked rather than assumed. The alternative on the consumer
side was --legacy-peer-deps, which silences every peer conflict in the tree
instead of the one that was actually understood.

Optional, because the domain imports no driver at all. post, postTransfer,
hashEntry, verifyChain and the money helpers are pure. A consumer that
wants the rules and brings its own storage should not have to install a
database driver to get them — which is precisely ClaimYour.Gold's case: it
computes hash chains with this package and writes through Prisma.

entries.title: Add a read-only reader over ClaimYour.Gold's existing ledger
entries.detail:
MongoLedgerStore writes this package's own format: hash-chained entries in
ledger_entries, integer minor units. ClaimYour.Gold's live ledger is not
in that format — gold_ledger has floating-point amounts, no chain, and a
different column set, holding years of real money. The two cannot be
swapped by changing a connection string.

The decision taken was to chain forward: new entries adopt the chained
format from a marked cutover; historical rows keep their shape and do not
claim a tamper-evidence they never had. This is the first half — anything
built on the LedgerStore port can read the live ledger today, with no
migration and no second query language.

It deliberately has no append, so it is not a LedgerStore. postEntry stays
the only writer of gold_ledger while both formats coexist, and a consumer
that tries to write fails to compile rather than at runtime against money.

headHash is always null. Inventing one would look like tamper-evidence to
every caller while proving nothing.

The float-to-minor conversion rounds rather than truncates: 12.34 in a
float column reads back as 12.339999999999998, and truncating loses a
whole minor unit per entry, always in the same direction.

verifyBalance answers the question nobody has been able to answer against
production data — whether wallet.goldBalance still equals the ledger.

13 tests against a fake collection, 100% line coverage. 55 tests total.

entries.title: Make the package installable
entries.detail:
private:true meant no repo could depend on this even in principle, which
is the actual reason "wire the consumers" never started — the blocker was
distribution, not code.

`prepare` matters more than it looks: npm runs it after installing from a
git URL, so dist/ gets built on the consumer's machine. Without it the
install succeeds and every import fails at runtime, a long way from the
cause.

publishConfig points at GitHub Packages for when a token exists. Git
dependencies work today with none.

entries.title: Add the MongoDB adapter, and a conformance suite that proves it interchangeable
entries.detail:
The single largest gap in this package: LedgerStore had one implementation and
it was in-memory, so nothing could run against real data.

WHAT THE DATABASE ENFORCES, RATHER THAN THIS FILE

Three of the port's guarantees are indexes, not code, because code here runs
once per process and an index runs on every write from every process forever:

  - idempotencyKey is unique, so a replay cannot become a second entry even
    when two processes race the same key at the same instant;
  - (identityId, assetId, previousHash) is unique, which is what stops two
    concurrent appends both building on the same chain head and silently
    forking history. It does not need to be partial: identityId and assetId
    are in the key, so "one entry with no predecessor" is scoped per chain
    rather than one null across the collection;
  - nothing updates or deletes, because no code path here issues either.

appendAll refuses a multi-entry batch when constructed without a MongoClient,
rather than writing a transfer half-way. Sessions need the client, and a torn
transfer is worse than a loud failure. Results are rebuilt inside the
transaction callback because withTransaction may retry it, and results from an
aborted attempt are not real.

Amounts are stored as strings and converted only at this boundary. Minor units
are integers that can outgrow a double over a long-lived ledger, and the domain
never sees a Mongo type.

THE CONFORMANCE SUITE

tests/conformance.test.ts runs the identical suite against every adapter. The
port is the seam the whole migration story rests on — a document database today,
a chain-backed store later, with the domain indifferent. "Indifferent" was an
intention; this makes it a build failure.

It skips Mongo unless MONGO_URL is set, so a laptop with no database still gets
the in-memory pass. CI provides one as a SINGLE-NODE REPLICA SET rather than a
standalone: sessions require a replica set, and a standalone would pass every
test here except the transfer ones

entries.title: Initial ledger: pure domain, storage behind a port
entries.detail:
An append-only, multi-asset settlement ledger. Flashy Gold is the first
asset on it rather than the thing itself; ore, stone and wheat are
configuration records, not new code paths.

Every design choice here answers a defect found in the predecessor's
production data:

  - Amounts are signed integers in minor units, because Float columns
    drift and 185 rows carried a sign that contradicted their own balance
    movement.
  - Transfers are two entries, because gifts and tips moved both wallets
    while writing nothing on either side.
  - Entries are append-only and content-hashed into a per-identity chain,
    because history you can edit is not evidence.
  - Writes are idempotent under a stable key, because retries are constant
    at scale and a double award is unrecoverable.

The domain is pure — no database, clock or randomness — and a lint rule
fails the build if that slips. All persistence sits behind LedgerStore,
which is the only thing a move onto different infrastructure, including a
chain, would have to reimplement.

32 tests, 99% coverage with the gate failing the build below threshold,
strict type-checked lint, and three ADRs recording why.
